strengths: Addresses a timely and important NLP systems problem: converting modern dense SwiGLU LLMs into sparsely activated MoEs without expensive continual pretraining.
Proposes a concrete pipeline combining activation profiling, shared/routed neuron separation, balanced expert assignment, an analytic initialization router, and optional lightweight LoRA adaptation.

Evaluation is reasonably broad, covering Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B, WikiText-2/C4 perplexity, six downstream tasks, end-to-end latency, calibration-data ablations, expert-configuration ablations, load balancing, extended SlimPajama fine-tuning, and a 13B scaling experiment.

CMoE consistently outperforms the compared LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 conversions under the same no-training or 2k-sample adaptation budget, and reports substantial full-model speedups of roughly 1.4–1.6x at 25% FFN activation.
The conversion itself is computationally cheap, requiring only a small calibration set, and the paper provides several useful hyperparameters and implementation details.
The overall framework is understandable and Figure 1 effectively communicates the conversion and inference process.
weaknesses: Several headline claims are not supported by the results. The 75% activation setting is called ‘lossless,’ yet after LoRA its perplexity remains substantially worse than dense: Llama-2 7B increases from 5.27 to 7.02 on WikiText-2 and from 7.27 to 10.98 on C4, while Llama-3 8B increases from 6.14 to 8.26 and from 9.44 to 17.06. Downstream accuracy also remains well below the dense models.

The training-free/immediate-deployment claim is weakly supported. Without fine-tuning, 25% activation yields very high perplexity, e.g. 62.30/136.12 for Llama-2 and 143.38/284.19 for Llama-3, while 75% activation can yield >60k or 10.16 WikiText perplexity. The evidence therefore suggests that fine-tuning is usually necessary for usable quality.

The claim that brief LoRA ‘recovers over 76% of the dense model’s downstream accuracy’ is misleading. That retention is not achieved across the suite; for example, after 25% fine-tuning, ARC-C and HellaSwag retain roughly 43–52% and 45–49% on Llama-2, and average task retention is only around 62–67% across the two models.

The analytic router derivation relies on strong, poorly validated approximations. Equation (3) assumes that neurons can be ranked by |h_i| while ignoring the magnitude of the down-projection vector; the later argument also replaces vector outputs with summed absolute values and assumes one representative neuron’s activation approximates the aggregate norm of an entire expert. No oracle-router, random-router, routing-accuracy, or reconstruction-error ablation is provided to justify these choices.

The term ‘differentiable router’ is overstated because hard TopK selection and the load-balancing bias are not differentiable; only the expert scales receive ordinary gradients. It is also unclear whether the router’s representative-neuron weights are fine-tuned or frozen, and the load-balance update rule is not fully specified.

Inference-speed evaluation is insufficiently reproducible. The paper does not report the GPU model, batch sizes, sequence lengths, precision, kernel implementation, inference mode, repetitions, or latency variance, and it does not precisely define the ‘memory-bound’ and ‘compute-bound’ regimes. The code URL is also blank.

The memory story needs clarification. Repartitioning FFN neurons does not reduce total parameter count or GPU memory capacity; it reduces active computation and potentially weight traffic. ‘Activating 25% of parameters’ should be stated as 25% of FFN expert parameters, since attention and other layers remain active and all experts may still need to reside in memory.

There is an important reproducibility inconsistency in the activation metric: the main text says K_a=10, while Appendix A reports histograms for K_a=1,000. The normalization applied to X, W_gate, and W_up before activation profiling is also underspecified, and these choices can materially change neuron grouping and router construction.

The empirical study would benefit from stronger baselines and ablations, including direct comparisons with MoEfication/XMoE-style upcycling, simpler activation-clustering routers, and multiple random seeds with uncertainty estimates. Evidence beyond Llama architectures is limited, and the 13B result reports only perplexity.

Presentation and notation require cleanup: the discussion of balanced versus unbalanced assignment is contradictory, several equation indices are confusing, q is not defined in the main method, and there are typos such as ‘dense matrix oo deease’ and a duplicated citation phrase. The novelty relative to MoEfication and LLaMA-MoE-v2 should also be stated more sharply.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely NLP problem: reducing FFN inference cost in dense LLMs without expensive continued pre-training.

The proposed design is practically motivated: frequently active neurons are placed in shared experts, sparsely co-activated neurons are grouped into routed experts, and the router can be initialized analytically before optional lightweight fine-tuning.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B, perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4, six downstream tasks, measured latency, calibration-size ablations, expert-configuration ablations, load balancing, and a larger-model appendix.
The training-free conversion is fast relative to continued pre-training, and the reported end-to-end speedups at 25% activation—if reproducible—would be practically useful.
The paper is generally well organized and the high-level framework in Figure 1 is understandable.
weaknesses: The central 'lossless perplexity' claim is contradicted by the results. For example, at 75% activation Llama-2 7B changes WikiText-2 perplexity from 5.27 to 7.02 without fine-tuning and 5.69 after fine-tuning; C4 changes from 7.27 to 10.21 and 10.98. Llama-3 8B shows similarly large gaps, including 9.44 versus 17.06 on C4 after fine-tuning. These are not lossless results.
The 25% activation claim of 'usable perplexity without additional training' is also overstated: training-free perplexity is 62.30/136.12 for Llama-2 and 143.38/284.19 for Llama-3 on WikiText-2/C4.

The analytical router derivation has a substantial conceptual gap. After the exact identity in Eq. (12), the paper replaces the norm of a sum by a sum of norms, ignores the magnitudes of the down-projection vectors, and assumes one representative neuron can predict the aggregate activation of an entire cluster. Moreover, Eqs. (14)–(16) appear to select experts according to input-independent expected activations, while Eq. (18) defines an input-dependent router; Eq. (19) does not establish that these are equivalent.

No direct evidence validates routing fidelity, such as correlation between the representative-neuron score and the actual norm of the omitted expert output, or comparison with random representative neurons, static routing, or simple magnitude-based routing.

The balanced-clustering formulation is presented inconsistently. Eq. (7) already enforces equal expert capacity and is a balanced transportation problem, but the text calls it unbalanced and introduces the matrix extension in Eq. (9). The indexing in Eqs. (9)–(10) also contains confusing notation and apparent typos, making the implementation difficult to verify.

The baseline comparison is not fully fair. LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 are methods that rely on training or post-training, but they are evaluated in training-free form or with only the proposed 2k-sample LoRA budget. This does not establish superiority over their intended pipelines. Additional training-free or compute-matched baselines, including random balanced grouping, are missing.

The speed evaluation lacks essential reproducibility details: GPU type, precision, batch size, sequence length, MoE kernel, routing overhead, memory usage, and latency variance are not specified. The reported 75%-activation full-model speedups are 1.02x and 1.12x, so the abstract's unspecified '5% acceleration' is not clearly supported.

The comparison with Pythia-1.0B and TinyLlama-1.1B is misleading because CMoE retains the entire dense 7B parameter set in memory; only the active parameter count is reduced. Unless expert weights are separately unloaded or sharded, the deployment memory footprint is not comparable to a 1B dense model.

The claim that brief fine-tuning recovers 'over 76%' of downstream accuracy is too broad. Several task-level retentions are far lower, for example Llama-2 at 25% activation retains roughly 49% on HellaSwag and 52% on ARC-Challenge relative to the dense model.

Robustness is limited. Calibration uses only eight WikiText-2 examples, and the appendix shows strong domain sensitivity: calibrating Llama-2 13B on C4 increases WikiText-2 perplexity substantially. Prompt formats, evaluation settings, random seeds, and variance for downstream experiments are also insufficiently documented.
Reproducibility is weakened by the blank code-release statement in the abstract and missing implementation details for the inference stack and some LoRA configuration choices.

The manuscript contains noticeable writing and citation problems, including a duplicated '[12] modifies [12] modifies' phrase, typographical errors, and an apparently incorrect WikiText citation: reference [29] is the Pointer Sentinel Mixture paper rather than the WikiText citation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and highly relevant problem in efficient LLM inference: converting dense FFNs into sparse MoEs without costly continual pre-training.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually clear and technically detailed: activation profiling with ATopK, separation into shared and routed experts, balanced expert assignment, analytical router construction, and optional lightweight adaptation.

The empirical evaluation covers two modern model families, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B, and includes perplexity, six downstream tasks, measured latency, expert-configuration ablations, and additional calibration and scaling analyses.

The main efficiency claim is promising: at 25% activation, CMoE reports roughly 1.5x end-to-end latency reduction while remaining functional without training, and lightweight LoRA fine-tuning provides substantial recovery.
The conversion is fast and calibration is inexpensive, and the promised code release could make the approach practically useful and reproducible.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated. The claimed 'lossless precision' at 75% activation is not supported by Table 1: after fine-tuning, Llama-2 7B has perplexity 5.69 versus 5.27 on WikiText-2 and 10.21 versus 7.27 on C4, while Llama-3 8B has 8.26 versus 6.14 and 17.06 versus 9.44. These should be described as approximate or task/model-specific trade-offs, not lossless.

The claimed '5% acceleration' is ambiguous. Table 3 reports different speedups depending on configuration and hardware regime, including 1.02x/1.05x for S3A9E16 and 1.05x/1.12x for S3A3E8; the exact configuration and regime must be specified.

The claim that 2,000 samples recover 'over 76% of the dense model's downstream accuracy' is not true as an aggregate statement. For Llama-2 at 25% activation, several relative recovery rates are far below 76%, such as ARC-C around 52% and HellaSwag around 49%. Task-wise and average recovery should be reported explicitly.

The router derivation relies on largely unvalidated approximations, particularly Equation (3), which ranks neuron outputs by hidden activation magnitude while ignoring the down-projection weights. The representative-neuron approximation of each cluster's expected activation also lacks error analysis or comparison with alternative router targets.

The described hard TopK routing is not fully differentiable with respect to router logits or the load-balancing bias. The paper does not explain whether a straight-through estimator, soft TopK, or another gradient approximation is used, so the differentiable-routing claim is unclear.

Inference-speed evaluation is under-specified for reproducibility: GPU model, precision, batch size, sequence length, software versions, kernels, warm-up procedure, repeated runs, and variance are not reported. The model also retains the dense model's total memory footprint, so comparisons based only on active parameters can be misleading.

The primary baselines were designed to use continual or post-training, so evaluating them in an untrained or 2k-sample setting may be a straw-man comparison. Direct comparison with other training-free upcycling methods would strengthen the contribution.

Table 4's comparison with smaller dense models is overclaimed: after 1.2B tokens, CMoE surpasses Pythia-1.0B on only one of the four reported tasks and still uses a much larger total model. The paper should clarify both active-parameter and total-memory costs.

The paper contains noticeable writing and bibliographic errors, including an incorrect WikiText citation, a duplicated '[12] modifies [12] modifies' phrase, several typos, inconsistent figure/equation references, and an apparently missing code URL.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: converting dense FFNs or existing MoE experts into sparse MoEs without continued pretraining, using only a small calibration set and lightweight LoRA fine-tuning.

The shared-versus-routed distinction is intuitive and well motivated by heterogeneous neuron activation frequencies, and the full pipeline—activation profiling, balanced clustering, representative-neuron routing, optional scaling, and load balancing—is clearly presented.

Experimental coverage is broad: four model families spanning 7B to 72B parameters, both dense and MoE models, five zero-shot benchmarks, and additional knowledge, coding, math, perplexity, calibration, clustering, data-efficiency, load-balancing, and orthogonality ablations.

The paper reports both quality and practical efficiency metrics, including FLOPs, MACs, throughput, construction time, token budget, context length, and memory-/compute-bound regimes, rather than relying only on parameter sparsity.

The hierarchical application to existing MoE models and demonstrated complementarity with neuron-level activation sparsity are useful extensions, and the authors explicitly acknowledge several scope limitations.
weaknesses: The supposedly analytical routing derivation is primarily heuristic. Equation (12) replaces |h_i w_down,i| by |h_i| without bounding variation in output-projection column norms, and the expert-level bound in Eqs. (22)–(24) omits the corresponding w_down,i norms. A single representative neuron selected by binary centroid similarity is also not proven to rank an expert’s total hidden-state or output contribution.

There is an important mismatch between the activation analysis and the experimental configuration. Figure 2 uses K_a=1000, whereas the experiments use K_a=10. For Llama-2-7B, K_a=10 implies a mean activation rate of roughly 10/11008≈0.0009, but S3A3E8 assigns 37.5% of neurons to always-computed shared experts. Many of these neurons cannot be consistently active. The paper should show the K_a=10 distribution across layers, the activation-rate cutoff for shared experts, and ablations in which the shared-expert size matches the observed high-frequency set.

Because SwiGLU/SiLU units are not exactly zero, activation sparsity is induced by magnitude-based top-K selection rather than measured directly. The bimodality evidence is mainly from one representative layer, so layer-wise and model-wide statistics are needed to establish that the claimed structure is generic.

Reproducibility is incomplete: I could not find a code-release statement, GPU/hardware specifications for the 4.5-minute/46-minute timings and throughput measurements, random seeds, or variance/confidence intervals. Expert kernels, batching, and routing overhead should also be specified to interpret the end-to-end speedups.

Baseline fairness is only partially convincing. Reimplemented MoE baselines restricted to 2k samples may not represent their originally trained performance, and the 20% structured-pruning comparison does not have identical sparsity semantics to 25% FFN-only sparsity. A dense model with matched LoRA tuning and simpler routing ablations would strengthen the claims.

The practical trade-off is more modest than some framing suggests. At 25% FFN sparsity there are non-trivial drops from the dense model—for example Llama-2-7B HellaSwag falls from 76.00 to 69.36 and ARC-Challenge from 46.16 to 40.35—while measured speedups range from about 1.02× to 1.17× and are small in memory-bound settings.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior activation-based upcycling, shared-expert MoEs, and co-activation clustering; the main contribution is the particular lightweight combination rather than a fundamentally new routing principle. Evaluation is also limited to English decoder-only models, as the authors acknowledge.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: converting pretrained dense FFNs into sparse MoE layers without expensive continual pretraining.
The proposed shared-expert/routed-expert decomposition is intuitive, and the framework is designed to apply both to dense models and recursively to existing MoE experts.

The empirical campaign is broad in scope, spanning Llama-2 and Qwen models at several scales, multiple zero-shot benchmarks, perplexity, calibration sensitivity, clustering/routing ablations, throughput, and hierarchical MoEs.

The paper compares favorably with several reimplemented MoE-construction baselines under a matched 2k-sample fine-tuning budget and provides evidence of substantially lower token and conversion-time cost.

The method is presented clearly, with an appendix describing the activation pipeline, balanced clustering, router construction, and optional fine-tuning, and the authors explicitly discuss several limitations.
weaknesses: A critical internal inconsistency undermines the activation-pattern evidence. With ATopK, the sum of all neuron activation rates must equal K_a per calibration token, so for K_a=10 the mean rate in Llama-2-7B is only about 10/11008. This is incompatible with Figure 2, generated with K_a=1000, where many neurons have rates near 0.07 and some approach 1. It is also incompatible with assigning 3 of 8 experts, or 4128 neurons, to a consistently active shared component. The paper must clarify whether K_a=10 is a typo, a percentage, or a different statistic and provide distributions for the setting actually used.

The analytical router derivation relies on unsupported approximations. Neuron output contribution is h_i w_down,i, but the method ranks neurons using only |h_i| and ignores variation in the down-projection weights. No bound, weight normalization, or empirical correlation is provided to justify this proxy.

The routing objective is not derived rigorously. The conversion from output reconstruction error to summed L1 hidden-state magnitudes uses a loose triangle-inequality relaxation, Eq. 8 omits an absolute value even though SwiGLU hidden activations can be negative, and Eq. 24 appears to rank experts by dataset-average activations, which are constant and cannot by themselves justify input-dependent routing.

The central bimodal-activation claim is based on a representative layer in one model and does not establish that the high-frequency group contains the 37.5% of neurons assigned to three shared experts. The natural mode size, layer-wise variation, and correspondence between the observed split and the chosen expert count are not analyzed.

The ablation evidence does not cleanly isolate the two main contributions. Table 5 replaces routers in prior grouping methods, but there is no controlled comparison of activation clustering without shared experts or parameter/weight clustering with shared experts. Sensitivity to K_a and balanced versus unbalanced clustering is also missing.

Some empirical claims are overstated. The method does not outperform every baseline on every task; for example, on Llama-2-7B ARC-E, EMoE scores 68.94 while the proposed method scores 58.63. Accuracy losses relative to the dense model can also be large, such as 74.58 to 58.63 on Llama-2-7B ARC-E and 57.88 to 48.80 on Qwen3-30B-A3B ARC-C.

The experiments lack statistical rigor: no multiple seeds, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported, despite many differences being around one percentage point. A dense model receiving the same 2k-sample LoRA treatment is also missing as a control.

Comparisons with LLaMA-MoE and similar methods under a 2k-sample budget demonstrate budget efficiency, but they do not establish superiority over those methods when used with their intended large-token training regimes. The strongest Table 1 results also depend on fine-tuning, while the training-free evaluation is limited to MMLU and perplexity.

The practical efficiency gain is modest. At 25% FFN sparsity, FLOPs decrease by only 16.6% and measured throughput by 14.8% on Llama-2-7B; the reported maximum 1.17x speedup occurs in a specialized compute-bound setting. Memory is not reduced, and memory-bound speedups are close to 1.0x.

Important deployment details are incomplete, including the inference kernel, hardware, batching policy, and full latency methodology. The k-sample self-consistency mitigation also multiplies generation compute by k and can substantially reduce or eliminate the reported speedup.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior activation-based FFN restructuring methods such as MoEfication and G-MoEfication. The main additions are the shared high-frequency expert and representative-neuron router, but their technical justification remains heuristic.

Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code and seeds and by resolving notation ambiguities, including the singular shared expert E^s versus N_s shared experts, binary gates versus real-valued fine-tuned gates, and the precise definition of sparsity used in the tables.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful structural distinction between frequently active and conditionally active FFN neurons, and exploits it to separate always-on shared experts from input-dependent routed experts. This is intuitive, well motivated by activation analyses, and applicable both to dense models and existing MoE models.

The proposed restructuring is training-light: activation profiling uses only eight calibration examples, the router is constructed analytically from representative neurons, and the full pipeline takes about 4.5 minutes before optional 2k-sample LoRA fine-tuning. This is a substantial practical advantage over methods requiring billions or hundreds of billions of continued-training tokens.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering Llama-2 7B/70B, Qwen-2.5 7B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B, with multiple zero-shot benchmarks as well as knowledge, coding, and math tasks. The method consistently outperforms reimplemented MoE-restructuring and structured-pruning baselines under the same 2k-sample adaptation budget.

The paper includes informative ablations on training-free versus fine-tuned performance, calibration source and size, clustering and routing choices, expert configurations, load balancing, hierarchical MoE restructuring, and compatibility with neuron-level activation sparsity. These ablations clarify which components contribute to the gains.

Efficiency is examined from several angles, including FLOPs, MACs, throughput, conversion time, token budget, memory-bound settings, and compute-bound settings. The reported 16.6% FLOP reduction and 14.8% throughput improvement for Llama-2 7B, with up to 1.17x speedup in a favorable Qwen-2.5 72B setting, suggest practical value.

The manuscript is clearly written and organized, and the appendix provides the activation pipeline, balanced clustering formulation, and router derivation. The limitations section is candid about calibration dependence, routing variance, and the current decoder-only/English scope.
weaknesses: The central claim that the router minimizes reconstruction error is only heuristically justified. Equations (12) and (23) replace neuron or expert outputs weighted by the down projection with hidden-activation magnitudes, without bounded-weight assumptions, error bounds, or direct empirical correlation. The representative neuron may not reliably approximate the summed output of its cluster because output direction, down-projection weights, and cancellation are ignored.

The evidence for the bimodal activation-frequency claim is limited in the main paper to a representative layer and model, and the statistic depends on the ATop-K ranking criterion rather than a natural activation threshold. Distributions across layers and models and sensitivity to K_a would make the motivation more convincing.

Although the method outperforms baselines under the matched 2k-sample regime, it does not fully preserve dense-model quality at 25% sparsity on several tasks. Conclusions about superiority should also be restricted to this low-budget post-training setting, since reimplemented baselines are not evaluated in their original large-scale training regimes.

Experimental reporting lacks repeated seeds, variance estimates, and significance tests. A dense baseline fine-tuned with the same LoRA budget would also help distinguish gains due to restructuring from gains due to task adaptation.

The deployment evidence is not yet complete. The headline 1.17x speedup is restricted to a high-batch, compute-bound Qwen-2.5 72B scenario, while the more general Llama-2 7B throughput gain is about 14.8%. Hardware, batching, custom-kernel details, gather/scatter overhead, and memory-bound latency should be specified, and quality is not reported jointly for the 72B speed benchmark.

The contribution is primarily an empirical engineering combination of known activation clustering and MoE construction ideas. Despite the term “analytical,” the router remains a proxy-based heuristic; stronger theoretical justification or weighted-output validation would raise confidence in its generality.

Code and artifact availability are not clearly stated in the manuscript. Releasing the implementation, calibration scripts, expert-configuration files, and benchmarking kernels would substantially improve reproducibility.
